patient.name: Sofia Rahman
patient.complaint: Recurrent one-sided throbbing headaches with flashing zig-zag lines beforehand
background: Takes the combined oral contraceptive pill
Junior doctor on night shifts in Whitechapel
Mild asthma as a child, none since age 12

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a recurrent unilateral throbbing headache lasting hours, nausea and photophobia, often with a reversible visual aura; red flags (thunderclap, meningism, persistent deficit) point elsewhere.

points: Sofia, 26: headaches twice a month for a year.
**Zig-zag flashing lines** spread across her vision for 20 minutes first.
Then a **left-sided throbbing** headache, worse on moving.
Vomits, hides in a **dark, quiet room**; lasts about 14 hours.

steps.lead: Recurrent, moderate to severe attacks with nausea and light sensitivity, some with aura: Sofia has a **primary headache disorder**.
Sofia's **night shifts** (sleep deprivation), her **mother's headaches** and her **pill** all fit the risk factors and CHOCOLATE triggers.
Sofia's headache is **unilateral, throbbing**, worse with movement, light and noise, with vomiting, lasting **4 to 72 hours**.

visual.title: How long does an attack last?
bands: under 4 h: think cluster or other
visual.label: Sofia 14 h
visual.caption: Cluster headache lasts 15 minutes to 3 hours; migraine lasts 4 to 72 hours.

points: Between attacks she feels completely well.

steps.lead: Sofia's zig-zags come **before** the headache and **fully reverse**, with a normal examination between episodes: classic **aura**. And she is on the **combined pill**.

steps.q: Sofia has migraine with aura and takes the combined pill. What is the key risk?
steps.r: The COCP plus migraine with aura significantly raises **ischaemic stroke** risk, so it is contraindicated (UKMEC 4).

steps.lead: Sofia has **no red flags**: no thunderclap onset, meningism or persistent deficit. **IIH** is the key differential if a headache is positional or atypical.

steps.text: Aura is **positive and spreading** (zig-zags, tingling marching up the arm) and fully reverses. Sudden **negative** loss (a blank field, a dead arm) suggests **TIA**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?': for typical migraine the answer is none (clinical diagnosis); imaging only appears when the stem gives a red flag.

steps.q: Sofia asks for a brain scan. What does she need?
steps.r: Migraine is a **clinical diagnosis**. With a normal examination and no red flags, imaging is not needed.

steps.lead: Sofia's history and normal examination **are** the diagnosis: no routine imaging. Only **red flags** would trigger tests for a secondary cause.

steps.title: Does this headache need investigating?
nodes: Yes → investigate for a secondary cause
steps.caption: Sofia goes down the 'No' branch.

points: Sofia keeps a **headache diary** for 8 weeks.
Attacks cluster after night shifts and weekend lie-ins.
Uses painkillers on 4 days a month.

steps.text: A new headache that is **sudden 'worst ever'**, with meningism or a persistent deficit, is not migraine until a **secondary cause** is excluded.
A **headache diary** (frequency, triggers, painkiller days) supports the diagnosis and spots **medication overuse**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': acute attacks get a triptan plus an NSAID or paracetamol; prophylaxis is propranolol or amitriptyline (topiramate avoided in women who could become pregnant); the combined pill is stopped in migraine with aura.

steps.q: What is the best acute treatment for Sofia's attacks?
o: Oral sumatriptan taken at the start of the aura
steps.r: **Combination**: triptan plus NSAID or paracetamol, taken once the **headache** starts, not during the aura. Propranolol is prophylaxis.

steps.lead: Sofia takes **sumatriptan 50 mg plus ibuprofen 400 mg** when the headache begins, with **metoclopramide** for her vomiting, and avoids her triggers.
If Sofia vomits her tablets, she can use **nasal or subcutaneous** sumatriptan. If she becomes pregnant, **paracetamol** is first-line.

points: Her **combined pill is stopped** (migraine with aura).
Switched to a **progestogen-only** method after discussion.
Six months later: attacks up to 5 a month, missing shifts.

steps.lead: Sofia's attacks are now frequent and disabling: she starts **propranolol** (her asthma resolved in childhood). **Topiramate** is avoided as she may want children.

visual.title: Sofia's migraine days per month
visual.caption: Prophylaxis takes weeks to work; review at 2 to 3 months before calling it a failure.

visual.title: Days per month Sofia takes a triptan
visual.label: Sofia 3 days
visual.caption: Triptans on 10 or more days a month (simple painkillers on 15 or more) risk medication overuse headache.

steps.title: Migraine management
nodes: Oral not tolerated: nasal or subcutaneous sumatriptan
Frequent attacks: propranolol or amitriptyline → topiramate or candesartan → rimegepant

steps.lead: Sofia's plan follows **NICE CG150** and **BASH** guidance: combination acute treatment, prophylaxis for frequent attacks, and review.

steps.text: Sumatriptan is contraindicated in **ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or MI, peripheral vascular disease and hypertension**. Check before prescribing.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the trigeminovascular system and CGRP, cortical spreading depression as the cause of aura, and how triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) and gepants work.

steps.lead: Sofia's pain comes from activated **trigeminal** nerve fibres releasing **CGRP** around meningeal vessels: neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation.
Sofia's zig-zags are a slow wave of **cortical spreading depression** moving across her occipital (visual) cortex, which is why they spread.
Sofia's scalp feels sore to brush during attacks: **sensitised** trigeminal and central pathways cause **allodynia**.

steps.q: How does sumatriptan relieve Sofia's headache?
steps.r: Triptans are **5-HT1B/1D agonists**: cranial vasoconstriction and less neuropeptide release. Gepants block CGRP; metoclopramide blocks D2.

steps.lead: Sumatriptan constricts Sofia's cranial vessels and stops **neuropeptide** release; rimegepant would block **CGRP** itself.
Sofia is warned: painkillers on too many days a month cause **medication overuse headache**.

mcq.q: How long does a typical migraine attack last?
mcq.r: Migraine lasts **4 to 72 hours**. 15 minutes to 3 hours suggests cluster headache.

mcq.q: Which mnemonic lists common migraine triggers?
mcq.r: **CHOCOLATE**: chocolate, hangovers, orgasms, cheese/caffeine, oral contraceptives, lie-ins, alcohol, travel, exercise.

mcq.q: Why is the combined pill contraindicated in migraine with aura?
mcq.r: Combined oestrogen plus migraine with aura significantly raises **ischaemic stroke** risk.

mcq.q: Which is the key differential for migraine with atypical, positional features?
mcq.r: The notes name **IIH** as the key differential with atypical (positional) features.
**Clinical diagnosis**; investigate only with red flags.

mcq.q: What is first-line acute treatment for migraine?
o: Oral triptan plus NSAID or paracetamol
mcq.r: **Combination** of a triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol.

mcq.q: Which is first-line migraine prophylaxis in a woman with asthma?
mcq.r: Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma; topiramate is teratogenic. **Amitriptyline** fits.

mcq.q: What is first-line acute treatment for migraine in pregnancy?
mcq.r: **Paracetamol** is first-line in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
**Cortical spreading depression**: a wave of depolarisation then suppressed activity.
Triptans are **5-HT1B/1D agonists**: cranial vasoconstriction and reduced neuropeptide release.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman has had recurrent headaches for 2 years. Each starts with 20 minutes of shimmering zig-zag lines spreading across her vision, followed by a right-sided throbbing headache with nausea and dislike of light, lasting a day. Her mother has similar headaches. Neurological examination between attacks is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: zig-zag lines spreading across her vision
dislike of light, lasting a day
steps.x: Recurrent, aura then unilateral throbbing pain with photophobia, lasting hours, family history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cluster lasts 15 minutes to 3 hours, around the eye, with autonomic signs.
IIH gives daily positional headache and papilloedema.
Tension-type is bilateral and pressing, without aura or vomiting.
TIA causes sudden negative symptoms with no headache pattern over years.

steps.x: **C. Migraine with aura.** Spreading positive visual aura, then unilateral throbbing pain.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman has had episodic left-sided throbbing headaches with nausea and photophobia for 5 years, each lasting about 12 hours. She is well between attacks. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Investigation question: does she need any?
Long-standing, typical pattern, normal examination: no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CT is for red flags such as thunderclap headache.
ESR is for suspected giant cell arteritis in over-50s.
LP is for suspected SAH or meningitis.
MRI is not needed without red flags.

steps.x: **E. No investigation.** Migraine is a clinical diagnosis.

technique.stem: A 28 year old woman has migraine with aura, with attacks twice a month. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has no other medical problems and does not smoke. Her BP is 114/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate change to her contraception?
o: Add aspirin to the combined pill
Stop the combined pill and offer progestogen-only contraception
Switch to a higher-oestrogen combined pill
Switch to the combined vaginal ring

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop the COCP**; offer a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method.

elim: Aspirin does not make oestrogen safe here.
Continuing exposes her to stroke risk.
More oestrogen means more risk.
The ring is still combined oestrogen.

steps.x: **C. Stop the combined pill.** Any combined oestrogen method is contraindicated.

technique.stem: A 22 year old man has migraine. Before each headache he sees a bright flickering spot that slowly expands into a shimmering arc over 20 minutes and then disappears. Neurological examination between attacks is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his visual symptoms?
o: Occlusion of the central retinal artery

steps.x: A slowly spreading, fully reversible positive phenomenon.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cortical spreading depression** across the occipital cortex.

elim: Retinal artery occlusion gives sudden painless monocular loss.
Optic neuritis gives painful reduced acuity for days.
Raised ICP gives papilloedema and transient obscurations.
Infarction would leave a permanent deficit.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has recurrent headaches for 3 years. Each is a left-sided throbbing pain, worse on climbing stairs, with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and noise. Attacks last 8 to 24 hours. She is well between them. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Recurrent unilateral throbbing headache lasting 4 to 72 hours, worse with activity, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, is migraine (here without aura).

steps.x: Unilateral, pulsating, worse with movement, photophobia, phonophobia, hours.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cluster lasts under 3 hours with autonomic eye signs.
No frequent analgesic use is described.
SAH is sudden 'worst ever', not recurrent over years.
Tension-type is bilateral, pressing, without vomiting.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has 4 episodes over a year in which tingling starts in his right fingers and spreads up his arm over 15 minutes, followed by a throbbing headache with nausea lasting 10 hours. Each resolves completely. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. Examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A sensory aura that spreads (marches) over minutes, fully reverses, and is followed by a migrainous headache is migraine with aura. TIA symptoms are sudden and negative.

steps.x: Diagnosis of transient neurological symptoms with headache.

clues: spreads up his arm over 15 minutes
steps.x: Slow spread, positive symptom, then headache, fully reversible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Radiculopathy gives neck pain and fixed dermatomal symptoms, not headache.
Focal seizures spread over seconds, not 15 minutes.
Glucose is normal.
TIA is sudden onset and negative (numbness, weakness).

steps.x: **D. Migraine with aura.** Spreading over minutes = aura.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman with migraine has had a headache on most days for 3 months. She takes co-codamol or sumatriptan on about 20 days each month. The headache is worse on waking. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her daily headache?
practice.e: Frequent use of acute migraine treatments (triptans or opioids on 10 or more days a month) causes medication overuse headache, a recognised complication of migraine treatment.

steps.x: Cause of a change to daily headache.
Painkillers on 20 days a month in a migraine patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Tumour would give progressive symptoms, papilloedema or deficit.
Cluster is short attacks around the eye.
Fundi are normal.
The analgesic overuse is the key clue.

steps.x: **D. Medication overuse headache.** Stop the overused drug.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman started a combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago. Since then she has had three episodes of unilateral throbbing headache with vomiting and photophobia, each lasting about a day. She sleeps normally and does not drink alcohol. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely trigger of her migraine?
practice.e: Oral contraceptives are among the CHOCOLATE triggers, and her attacks began after starting the pill; she sleeps normally and does not drink.

clues: started a combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago
sleeps normally and does not drink alcohol
steps.x: New attacks began with the pill; other triggers excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: She does not drink.
No caffeine change is described.
No link to exercise is given.
She sleeps normally.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 6 year history of migraine with visual aura. She sees her GP between attacks for a review. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. She feels completely well today.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination today?
practice.e: Migraine aura is fully reversible and the neurological examination is normal between episodes. A persistent deficit is a red flag for a secondary cause.

steps.x: Aura is reversible; interictal exam is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Papilloedema suggests IIH or a mass.
A fixed field defect means a structural lesion.
Drift is a persistent deficit (red flag).
Horner's suggests cluster or carotid dissection.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman with migraine is reviewed after starting a new medication for frequent attacks. She reports tingling in her fingers and has lost 4 kg. She has stopped her contraception. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her new symptoms?
practice.e: Topiramate causes paraesthesia, weight loss and a mild metabolic acidosis, and is teratogenic, so it needs highly effective contraception. Amitriptyline causes weight gain.

steps.x: Paraesthesia, weight loss, low bicarbonate; contraception matters because it is teratogenic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amitriptyline causes weight gain and drowsiness.
Candesartan causes dizziness and hyperkalaemia.
Propranolol causes cold hands and fatigue.
Rimegepant is not linked to acidosis or paraesthesia.

steps.x: **E. Topiramate.** And it must not be used without highly effective contraception.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with nausea and photophobia, each lasting about 12 hours, for 4 years. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal. She asks whether she needs a brain scan. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis: with a typical history and normal examination, no investigation is needed. Investigate only for red flags.

practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to support the diagnosis?

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has migraine without aura, with attacks twice a month. Paracetamol alone does not help. She has no other medical problems. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate acute treatment?
practice.e: First-line acute treatment is combination therapy: an oral triptan with an NSAID or paracetamol. Propranolol and topiramate are prophylaxis; rimegepant is after two triptans fail.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Opioids are avoided in migraine (overuse, nausea).

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with migraine vomits within minutes of every attack starting, even after an antiemetic, and brings up her oral sumatriptan. She has no cardiovascular disease. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: When oral treatment is not tolerated, a non-oral triptan (nasal or subcutaneous sumatriptan) is used. A higher oral dose would still be vomited.

Triptan works but cannot be kept down; no contraindication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: A higher oral dose will be vomited too.

practice.q: Which is the most appropriate prophylactic treatment?
practice.e: Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma and topiramate is teratogenic in women of childbearing age, so amitriptyline is the first-line choice.

steps.x: Asthma excludes propranolol; no contraception excludes topiramate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

Rimegepant is third-line prophylaxis.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has migraine without aura. Her GP prescribes oral sumatriptan to take at the onset of headache, with ibuprofen. She has no cardiovascular disease. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of sumatriptan?
practice.e: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists, causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibiting trigeminal neuropeptide release. CGRP antagonism is how gepants work.

glossary.Migraine: A primary headache disorder with recurrent attacks of moderate to severe headache, often with nausea and light sensitivity.
glossary.Aura: Fully reversible neurological symptoms, usually visual, that precede a migraine headache.
glossary.Scotoma: A patch of lost or altered vision.
glossary.Photophobia: Discomfort or pain caused by light.
glossary.Primary headache: A headache disorder that is not caused by another condition, such as migraine or cluster headache.
glossary.Secondary headache: A headache caused by another condition, such as haemorrhage, infection or raised pressure.
glossary.CHOCOLATE: Mnemonic for migraine triggers: chocolate, hangovers, orgasms, cheese/caffeine, oral contraceptives, lie-ins, alcohol, travel, exercise.
glossary.COCP: Combined oral contraceptive pill, containing oestrogen and progestogen.
glossary.Combined oral contraceptive pill: Oestrogen plus progestogen pill; contraindicated in migraine with aura because of stroke risk.
glossary.Progestogen-only: Contraception without oestrogen, such as the progestogen-only pill, implant or hormonal coil.
glossary.UKMEC: UK criteria grading how safe each contraceptive is for a given condition; 4 means unacceptable risk.
glossary.IIH: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: raised brain pressure without a mass, causing headache and papilloedema.
glossary.Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: Raised intracranial pressure without a mass, usually in young overweight women; a key migraine differential.
glossary.Papilloedema: Swelling of the optic discs from raised intracranial pressure.
glossary.Meningism: Neck stiffness, photophobia and headache from meningeal irritation.
glossary.Thunderclap: A sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute; suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage.
glossary.Cluster headache: Severe unilateral headache around the eye lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, with a red watery eye.
glossary.Tension-type headache: A bilateral, pressing, band-like headache without vomiting or aura.
glossary.Triptan: A 5-HT1B/1D agonist used to treat acute migraine attacks.
glossary.Sumatriptan: The commonest triptan, taken orally, nasally or by subcutaneous injection.
glossary.Rimegepant: An oral CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) for acute treatment or prevention of migraine.
glossary.CGRP: Calcitonin gene-related peptide: a neuropeptide driving neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation in migraine.
glossary.Metoclopramide: A dopamine antagonist antiemetic that also speeds gastric emptying.
glossary.Extrapyramidal side effects: Drug-induced movement problems such as dystonia, more likely in young women on dopamine antagonists.
glossary.Propranolol: A non-selective beta-blocker; first-line migraine prophylaxis, contraindicated in asthma.
glossary.Amitriptyline: A tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for migraine prophylaxis.
glossary.Topiramate: An anticonvulsant used as second-line migraine prophylaxis; teratogenic.
glossary.Candesartan: An angiotensin receptor blocker used as second-line migraine prophylaxis.
glossary.Prophylaxis: Regular treatment taken to reduce the frequency of attacks.
glossary.Teratogenic: Able to cause birth defects when taken in pregnancy.
glossary.Trigeminovascular system: Trigeminal nerve fibres supplying meningeal blood vessels; their activation drives migraine pain.
glossary.Cortical spreading depression: A slow wave of neuronal depolarisation then suppressed activity across the cortex; the cause of aura.
glossary.Allodynia: Pain from a normally painless touch, such as brushing the hair.
glossary.Neurogenic inflammation: Inflammation caused by neuropeptides released from sensory nerve endings.
glossary.Medication overuse headache: Chronic daily headache caused by frequent use of acute headache treatments.
glossary.Headache diary: A record of attacks, triggers and painkiller use that supports the diagnosis.
glossary.Status migrainosus: A migraine attack lasting more than 72 hours.
glossary.TIA: Transient ischaemic attack: sudden, brief, negative focal neurological symptoms from ischaemia.
